abstract.p: Background: Reconfigurable manufacturing systems (RMSs) enable rapid adaptation of machines, tools, and control software to produce different part families. Objectives: This paper addressed a Multiple Part Family Production (MPFP) problem selecting the best reconfiguration policy (RP) when switching production between part families. RPs are represented as sequences of reconfiguration steps and evaluated by number of setups, total reconfiguration cost, and total reconfiguration time. This work presented a conceptual digital twin (DT) based framework for forming RP applicable to reconfigurable flow line (RFL). Method: This framework describes how a DT can model candidate reconfiguration sequences by using real or historical data to estimate time and cost, and support virtually in what if analyses for policy comparison prior to physical changes. The manuscript focuses on framework design, required data flows, and decision logic rather than on implementation or experimental deployment. Results: This work provides a structured DT architecture which acts as reconfiguration decision making tool for engineering managers and a formal representation of reconfiguration policies and evaluation metrics, and a roadmap for integrating data sources, simulation components, and validation procedures. A worked example is also presented to demonstrate how the proposed framework supports a management decision. Illustrative results show that RP$_1$ and RP$_3$ require only one reconfiguration, whereas RP$_2$ incurs an additional change at Stage 3. Consequently, RP$_1$ is the most efficient policy, followed by RP$_3$, while RP$_2$ imposes the highest reconfiguration burden. Conclusion: This work proposes a novel DT-driven RP for MPFP, applicable to an RFL, integrating real-time data analytics into RMS to manage reconfigurable machine tool (RMT) configurations across four production stages. The selected RP is intended to improve delivery performance, capacity utilization, production continuity, and system availability by minimizing setups and reconfiguration time/cost, thereby reducing downtime and maintaining a smoother production flow.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: In the current era of industrial transformation driven by Industry 4.0, manufacturing organizations are under immense pressure to continuously innovate, adapt, and respond to unpredictable changes in product demand and customer expectations. The intense global competition and shrinking product life cycles compel manufacturers to adopt systems that can reconfigure rapidly with minimal cost and disruption [1]. Traditional production systems designed for long production runs and stable product lines lack the flexibility required to cope with these new operational realities. Consequently, a reconfigurable manufacturing system (RMS) has emerged as a modern production paradigm capable of balancing high productivity with flexibility and responsiveness [2].

Unlike dedicated or flexible manufacturing systems, an RMS is explicitly designed for cost-effective reconfiguration both in terms of hardware and software allowing manufacturers to produce a variety of product families using modular and scalable configurations [2]. The core philosophy is that a reconfigurable system can swiftly alter its production capacity and functionality, maintaining efficiency under varying product mixes and volumes.

sec.title: 1.1. The role of reconfiguration in multi-part family production
sec.p: A part family represents a group of products sharing similar design or manufacturing features [3]. In a reconfigurable production environment, these families are produced sequentially across a reconfigurable flow line (RFL), which consists of several stages equipped with reconfigurable machine tools (RMTs) capable of performing multiple operations after minimal setup changes [4]. However, when switching from one part family to another, a part of flow line or the entire one must be reconfigured to align with the operational requirements of the next family. This changeover entails setup time, cost, and resource utilization that directly influence overall production efficiency [5].

Thus, determining an optimal reconfiguration policy (RP) that defines the sequence and method of switching between part families becomes a crucial decision-making problem. The goal is to minimize reconfiguration time, reduce cost, and limit the number of setup transitions without compromising the system’s responsiveness or production throughput. Inefficient sequencing can lead to unnecessary setup operations, higher energy consumption, and idle resource time, ultimately increasing total operational cost.

sec.title: 1.2. Need for adaptive reconfiguration-policy selection
sec.p: Traditional heuristic or deterministic scheduling models often fail to adapt to the stochastic nature of RMS environments where demand fluctuations and configuration dependencies are frequent. Adaptive algorithms can continuously evaluate real-time parameters such as reconfiguration effort, operation compatibility, and setup interdependencies to update the RP for each required transition within a predetermined part-family production order [6]. These algorithms employ feedback-driven decision mechanisms, making them more suitable for environments with variable product mix, uncertain demand, and limited setup data.

The present study addresses this critical research gap by introducing an adaptive algorithm for Multiple part family production (MPFP) in RFL. The algorithm integrates a set of adaptive decision rules to select the best RP that minimizes the total reconfiguration burden quantified through a multi-objective performance function combining reconfiguration count, reconfiguration cost, and reconfiguration time. The algorithm is termed adaptive because it updates the RP rather than the production sequence in response to changes in demand, shop‑floor disturbances, or updated performance criteria. It involves the decision rules that re‑evaluate reconfiguration count, reconfiguration cost, and reconfiguration time whenever new data or disruptions occur, ensuring that the selected RP remains suitable under changing operating conditions. Additionally, the integration with digital twin (DT) enables autonomous monitoring and real‑time adjustment, allowing the system to continuously adapt to environmental and demand variations while minimizing the overall reconfiguration burden.

sec.title: 1.3. Part family formation and sequencing in reconfigurable manufacturing systems
sec.p: An RMS is typically composed of RMTs arranged in modular configurations capable of performing multiple operations with minor physical or software-level adjustments. The ability to add, remove, or rearrange modules provides significant competitive advantage in environments characterized by high product variety and variable demand. Several studies have demonstrated that RMSs improve system responsiveness, reduce production lead times, and enhance resource utilization [7], [8].

The foundation of RMS planning lies in the part family formation (PFF) process of grouping components with similar manufacturing characteristics [9]. Once part families are identified, the production of multiple families on an RFL requires systematic sequencing to minimize reconfiguration overheads. Each part family demands a specific sequence of operations across multiple RMTs. When switching from one family to another, setup adjustments including tool changes, fixture reconfigurations, and control parameter modifications are required [10]. Researchers have addressed the sequencing and reconfiguration problem in RMS from different perspectives. Moghaddam et al. [11] proposed a configuration design model for scalable RMS considering variable product demand over its life cycle. Huang et al. [12] proposed a reconfiguration-aware similarity coefficient for grouping RMS parts into families through hierarchical clustering, while Xia et al. [13] developed a maintenance-oriented RP integrating system reliability and cost trade-offs. These works emphasize the importance of timely reconfiguration and sequence optimization to ensure cost-effective transitions between product variants.

sec.title: 1.4. Fundamental concept of digital twin
sec.p: DTs represent a cutting-edge data-driven approach combining real-time analytics, optimization, and simulation. A DT includes two main parts: a physical component and a virtual counterpart linked through real-time data link, with the virtual part holding detailed information about the physical component manufactured. DTs process vast amounts of real-time and offline data to improve system transparency. This enables extensive information usage for monitoring, predicting, diagnosing, simulating, and optimizing [14]. Some of the features of DT are presented as below:

sec.title: 1.4.1 Definition
sec.p: A virtual representation of a physical asset, system, or process that updates and interacts with real-world data in real time to optimize performance and decision-making.
• Components: Physical asset/data sources; Virtual model; Data integration layer; Analytics & artificial intelligence (AI).
• Capabilities: Simulation & forecasting; Performance optimization; Remote monitoring; Lifecycle management.
• Services: Asset performance management; Process optimization; Anomaly detection; Simulation & data visualization.
• Applications: Tracking system condition; Generating predictions; Diagnosis; Simulation and optimization.

sec.title: 1.5. Objectives and research contribution
sec.p: This research aims to support production/operations and engineering managers in selecting and scheduling reconfiguration policies for MPFP. The proposed DT evaluates feasible RMT configurations and part family-transition sequences by jointly considering setup frequency, reconfiguration time, reconfiguration cost, production capacity, and operational constraints, thereby supporting production planning, resource allocation, downtime control, and continuity of operations. The specific objective of this research is to design a computationally efficient adaptive sequencing approach for DT-driven MPFP in RMS environments that:
• Models cost, time, and frequency interdependencies.
• Identifies the optimal RP for each transition within a fixed part‑family production sequence, ensuring minimal reconfiguration effort.
• Improves responsiveness and ensures consistent throughput during changeovers.

The principal contribution is a DT-based managerial decision-support framework that converts real-time and historical shop-floor data into recommendations for selecting, timing, and authorizing partial or complete reconfiguration actions. An illustrative example is presented in section 5 to exhibit how the projected framework supports a management decision. It enables managers to compare alternative policies before implementation and allocate RMTs, labor, tools, fixtures, and production time while balancing cost, capacity, changeover downtime, delivery requirements, and uninterrupted flow.

sec.title: 1.6. Related works
sec.p: The presented body of work collectively demonstrates that integrating DT technology with RMS substantially advances the capability to plan, evaluate, and execute reconfiguration for MPFP while explicitly accounting for reconfiguration cost and time. Key themes emerging from the reviewed works are (1) real-time mapping and model fidelity; (2) optimization and decision-making under disturbance; (3) decentralized and learning-enabled reconfiguration; and (4) explicit treatment of cost/time trade‑offs and rapid virtual validation.

sec.title: 1.6.1 Real-time mapping and model fidelity
sec.p: High-fidelity, real-time DTs are foundational for effective reconfiguration management. Several studies emphasize the need to represent dynamic station and line behavior accurately in virtual space to enable reliable planning and execution [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]. Accurate mapping of reconfigurable stations and machines into the DT permits virtual prototyping, parallel virtual–real control, and predictive simulation of multiple product variants [15], [18], [20]. Maintaining and improving model fidelity through incremental learning on process data further strengthens reconfiguration decision quality and reliability [19].

sec.title: 1.6.2 Optimization and decision-making under disturbance
sec.p: In order to improve throughput and performance in the face of disturbances, it is done by generating near-instantaneous reconfiguration plans. Frameworks combining DT monitoring with rapid configuration optimization have demonstrated the ability to recover throughput losses and to search large configuration spaces quickly [16]. High-speed simulation coupled with capability-based resource models supports rapid evaluation of candidate configurations and selection under time constraints [16]. Analytical and optimization approaches, such as analytical target cascading, multi-objective cuckoo algorithms were applied to jointly handle order scheduling, balancing, and buffer sizing alongside reconfiguration decisions [18], [21]. In this work, the reconfiguration decision is supposed to be made by the production/operations manager, supported by the proposed DT-based decision framework. It is primarily a tactical decision, because it concerns selecting and scheduling reconfiguration policies between part families, while being informed by operational data and constraints.

sec.title: 1.6.3 Decentralized, multi-agent, and learning-enabled approaches
sec.p: Decentralized and learning-based controllers provide scalable alternatives to centralized planning when layout, agent heterogeneity, or dynamic tasks complicate the reconfiguration. Multi-agent cooperative swarm learning and decentralized decision architectures reported reduce layout compactness, processing time, and rearrangement cost [22]. Reinforcement learning methods applied through DT-driven environments enable online discovery of reconfiguration policies that incorporate moving, processing, and reconfiguration costs into the reward structure [23]. Combining continuous model updates through learning with reconfiguration management yields progressively improved planning outcomes [19].

sec.title: 1.6.4 Explicit modeling of reconfiguration cost and time
sec.p: Other works explicitly modeled reconfiguration cost and reconfiguration time as optimization objectives or constraints, reflecting their practical importance in MPFP [18], [21], [23]. Treating reconfiguration holistically integrating physical reconfiguration effort, moving costs, and processing impacts enables generation of minimal or cost‑aware reconfiguration solutions and supports trade-off analysis between immediate performance gains and reconfiguration overhead [17], [21]. Predictive estimation of reconfiguration time points i.e., scheduling when to reconfigure further reduces completion times and overall reconfiguration cost in production planning [18].

sec.title: 1.6.5 Rapid virtual validation and variant design
sec.p: The DT facilitates virtual validation of layout and variant designs prior to physical changes, reducing waste and accelerating changeovers [15], [20], [21], [22]. Use cases in electronics and smart-phone assembly illustrate the DT’s role in enabling fast variant design iterations, virtual verification of feasibility, and quantification of expected performance or cost impacts [20], [21]. High-fidelity 3D representations and fast simulation support both layout optimization and detailed evaluation of reconfiguration costs for MPFP [22].

sec.title: 1.6.6 Synthesis and gaps
sec.p: Few past studies proposed an evolutionary ecosystem in which DTs act as the central enabler linking monitoring, simulation, optimization, and learning for RMS reconfiguration. Effective systems combine real-time DT mapping, capability-aware resource models, rapid simulation, and optimization algorithms that explicitly account for reconfiguration cost and time, while leveraging decentralized and learning-based methods for scalability and adaptability. Remaining challenges suggested by the works include standardized metrics for trade-off evaluation across cost/time/performance dimensions, integration of human factors during semi-automatic reconfiguration, and systematic approaches to guarantee DT model validity over long-term deployments issues. Future works should address to make reconfiguration solutions robust in large-scale MPFP environments [17], [19].

sec.title: 1.8. Research gaps
sec.p: Despite considerable progress, several research gaps remain unresolved in the area of RMS sequencing and reconfiguration planning:

1. Limited consideration of multi-objective dependencies: Most previous studies optimize either reconfiguration cost or time, but rarely integrate both along with setup frequency in a unified decision model.
2. Static reconfiguration-policy assumptions: Many models evaluate reconfiguration alternatives using fixed input data and do not update policy selection when the system state changes.
3. Inadequate scalability: Existing algorithms often struggle to handle high part family diversity or stochastic variations in real-world production lines.
4. Lack of integration with DT: The conventional approaches are not designed to operate with DT frameworks that demand real-time adaptation and self-learning capabilities.

Consequently, there is a need for a DT-based decision-support procedure that can continuously assess and update reconfiguration policies within a predetermined part-family production order by considering changing operating conditions and multiple performance measures.

The paper addresses a multi‑criteria engineering management challenge of selecting RPs for MPFP in an RFL, requiring managers to balance reconfiguration time, cost, and number of set‑ups while meeting throughput and technological constraints. The study further shows how a DT‑driven decision process supports this selection by enabling systematic planning, comparison, and governance of reconfiguration actions for successive part-family transitions under diverse performance criteria and operational constraints.

The remainder of the paper is structured into several sections i.e., Section 2 focuses on the methodology; Section 3 presents the framework for DT-driven RP for MPFP; Section 4 presents the Mathematical formulation; Section 5 presents an illustration for demonstrating managerial decision support; Section 6 include discussion, while Section 7 concludes with major findings and Section 8 provides limitations of the work and directions for future research.

sec.title: 2.1. Assumptions
sec.p: The following assumptions are made in this work:
(i). Deterministic demand for each of the five-part families (which may differ) and a predefined production sequence, while the proposed procedure selects the RP for each required family transition.

(ii). The RFL is modeled as a sequential system in which stages may operate concurrently on different units, subject to sufficient intermediate-buffer capacity; buffer capacities are assumed fixed and non-constraining in the baseline framework.

(iii). To isolate reconfiguration-policy effects, machine failures, unplanned maintenance, and worker-availability constraints are excluded; equipment and personnel are assumed available, with such disruptions identified as extensions for future DT implementation.
(iv). Changing from one configuration to another is bi-directional and thus has the same time and cost in reverse transition.
(v). The order of families is fixed, and adaptation applies only to policy selection under changing conditions.
(vi). Production time is calculated only for capacity and throughput-feasibility checking. It is not included as an optimization criterion in the objective function.

Since multiple RMT configurations may be capable of executing the same operation, it becomes essential to evaluate and select the configuration that minimizes installation and/or reconfiguration cost while also ensuring rapid adaptability. The Reconfiguration path thus defines the sequence of transitions required when shifting from one family’s production setup to another. sec.title: 2.2. Introduction of the digital twin-based multiple part family production framework in factory settings
sec.p: A manufacturing enterprise introducing the DT‑based MPFP framework would collect real‑time machine states, tool and fixture identifiers, part‑family operation requirements, cycle times, and historical reconfiguration logs. These data streams are pre‑processed at the edge (cleaning, mapping, and timestamp synchronization) before being transferred to the Knowledge Database through standard industrial middleware such as Open Platform Communications-Unified Architecture (OPC-UA) or Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT). The DT uses this processed information to evaluate candidate reconfiguration policies and generate recommendations consistent with the performance criteria of reconfiguration time, reconfiguration cost, and number of setups.

The DT-based MPFP framework involves interaction of DT with shop‑floor devices through a data‑integration layer that links sensors, RMT controllers, and the Knowledge Database with the virtual simulation environment. A lightweight decision‑support interface presents the recommended RP to factory personnel. Decision authority follows a simple governance structure: Operators execute approved changeovers, line supervisors authorize partial reconfigurations, and engineering managers approve full configuration transitions. This workflow ensures that DT‑generated recommendations are reviewed and validated before physical implementation.

sec.title: 3. Digital twin-driven reconfiguration policy for multiple part family production
sec.p: The flow chart for creating an RP in MPFP within RMS is shown in Figure 1. The first step is to identify the part families and the order in which they will be processed. Then, it is checked whether all part families have already been produced. If not, the first unfinished part family must be produced. Before production begins, it is verified if a configuration change is needed at the production stage. If a change is required, it should follow these rules:
(a). Keep the number of setup changes as low as possible.

(b). If a set‑up change is necessary, it should be done in a way that minimizes the number of reconfigurations, the time taken, and the cost involved. Part families should be produced using the less expensive RMT configurations that can still perform the required operations.

If no configuration change is needed on the RFL, the part family is produced using the current setup. If a change is required, it must follow the two rules mentioned earlier. After the configuration is updated, the part family is produced. Once production of that family is finished, another check is made to see if all part families are completed. This cycle repeats until the last part family has been produced.

Figure 1 depicts physical changeovers which are monitored using digital work instructions, sensor feedback, and stepwise verification checkpoints. Each RMT transition is validated and recorded in the Knowledge Database to refine future DT predictions. If deviations occur, the system triggers a short planned interruption window to maintain safe and controlled reconfiguration. This monitoring loop ensures that DT‑recommended policies translate into reliable on‑floor execution.

sec.title: 3.1. Operation sequences selection of multiple part family production using the adaptive algorithm
sec.p: In an RFL with four production stages, five part families are scheduled for production in a defined order. The adaptive algorithm updates the RP for a fixed part‑family order; it does not determine the production sequence. Each family requires specific operations, which differ in type, sequence (Table 2), and the possible RMT configurations that can perform them (Table 5). The same operation may be executed by different RMT configurations, but these vary in production rates (Table 3). Therefore, the most suitable RMT configuration must be selected. Once all the operations on a part family are completed, the next family is prepared for processing. Since the requirements of the subsequent family differ from the previous one, the production stages must be reconfigured accordingly. The choice of reconfiguration time and cost (Table 4) significantly influences the overall effectiveness of the RMS. Thus, when shifting from a part family to another, the two previously stated guidelines must be applied.

Consider a MPFP sequence presented in a generic form\(\ f_{j} \rightarrow f_{j'} \rightarrow f_{j''} \rightarrow f_{j'''}\), processed across the four stages of the RFL. These stages are equipped with suitable RMT configurations capable of performing certain required operations. A multi‑level RP, comprising levels (i)\(\ f_{j} \rightarrow f_{j'}\), (ii) \(f_{j'} \rightarrow f_{j''}\ \)and (iii) \(f_{j''} \rightarrow f_{j'''}\), is applied as per the guidelines outlined earlier. The corresponding minimum reconfiguration time and cost are presented in Table 4. Likewise, reconfiguration policies can be suggested for other MPFP sequences as well.

Part families with similar operation sequences can be produced consecutively with minimal or no changeovers. However, part families with entirely different production requirements demand major setup changes on the RFL, which increases the number of reconfigurations, as well as the associated time and cost.

sec.title: 6. Discussion
sec.p: The proposed conceptual DT‑based framework for selecting RPs in MPFP builds on existing research showing how DTs can support decision‑making in RMS. Additionally, the selected RPs are not only a machine-configuration solution; selecting them is a tactical production-management decision that determines when resources are withdrawn, reassigned, or returned to production during family changeovers. By minimizing unnecessary setups and balancing reconfiguration time and cost against production requirements, the framework can support capacity utilization, delivery reliability, downtime reduction, and continuity of operations; however, these benefits remain to be empirically validated because the present study is conceptual and has not yet been deployed or experimentally benchmarked.

The framework integrates the system by linking RMT configurations with real‑time DT data flows, allowing configuration states, operation requirements, and transition costs to be continuously synchronized. These data streams feed a managerial decision layer that evaluates feasible reconfiguration policies against operational objectives such as throughput, downtime, and cost. Together, physical resources, information flows, and decision authority operate as a single coordinated mechanism for selecting and governing reconfiguration actions.

By presenting an illustrative example in Section 5, the framework provides clearer planning and authorization workflows by structuring how managers evaluate and approve reconfiguration actions. Its coordinated use of DT data reduces unnecessary downtime through timely, evidence‑based configuration updates. By formalizing the comparison of alternative policies, it enables a consistent and transparent evaluation process that strengthens operational decision‑making.

In relation to this work, another work [15] developed a DT approach aimed at reducing setup times in mixed‑model flow lines. The proposed DT evaluated different station configurations and recommends the sequence of changes that minimizes changeover time and the resulting downtime for operators. Their findings show that using a DT to test different setup options in advance can noticeably reduce the time needed for actual physical reconfiguration. This supports the idea that reconfiguration policies expressed as sequences of reconfiguration steps should first be evaluated in the DT environment before being applied on the real system, using metrics such as number of setups, total reconfiguration time, and total reconfiguration cost [15].

Fu et al. [16] expanded this concept by applying DTs to handle unexpected disturbances in smart manufacturing. Their DT framework continuously monitors the production line for disruptions; creates alternative line configurations using an optimization module; and quickly tests these options through simulation. This approach helped in recovering up to 63% of lost throughput during disturbance events. Results show that DT‑driven reconfiguration can keep production running and maintain system availability even when conditions change. Their findings support the inference of the present work i.e., the chosen RP should improve delivery performance, capacity use, and production continuity by reducing setups and reconfiguration time and cost. However, while Fu et al. focused on reconfiguration triggered by disturbances, the current study generalizes the decision problem to MPFP, where reconfiguration is planned in advance when switching between part families rather than caused by unexpected events.

Another DT framework specifically for reconfiguration management, emphasized a conceptual architecture and evaluation rather than full‑scale deployment [17]. Their framework defined modules for data acquisition, model management, reconfiguration planning, and evaluation, and demonstrated through case studies how DT‑based reconfiguration management can systematically compare alternative policies. This research is closely aligned with the contribution of present work of a structured DT architecture that acts as a reconfiguration decision‑making tool for engineering managers, and a formal representation of RPs and evaluation metrics [17]. A conceptual focus is linked with the present study that it provides roadmaps for integrating data sources, simulation components, and validation procedures, rather than detailed implementation of algorithms or hardware integration, reinforcing the legitimacy of a conceptual, architecture‑oriented contribution.

A DT‑based method was developed to predict reconfiguration time points in RMS [18]. Their approach used DT models to forecast when reconfiguration should occur and how long it will take, thereby reducing uncertainty in planning and scheduling. The reported results showed alignment between planned and actual reconfiguration times, which directly supported this study’s emphasis on using real or historical data within the DT to estimate reconfiguration time and to compare candidate RPs on this basis [18].

A DT with self‑organized reconfiguration management, built on an adaptive process model [19], showed why DTs need to be flexible and able to update themselves as conditions change. Such adaptive, feedback‑driven DTs can revise their internal process models and make reconfiguration decisions automatically. This supported the idea that a DT‑based reconfiguration‑policy framework should not only store fixed reconfiguration sequences, but also adjust how it evaluates those sequences whenever new data such as updated processing times or failure rates becomes available.

Another DT‑based method [20] designed and evaluated different configuration and layout variants for an assembly line producing computer, communication, and consumer electronics (3C) products. Their DT models allow rapid testing of design options before making physical changes, which reported shortened development time and improved decisions, especially when many product variants must be handled. This idea is similar to the MPFP context, where multiple product families require frequent reconfiguration. Their work is in line with the view that DTs can model and compare candidate reconfiguration sequences using historical and real‑time data, enabling “what‑if” analysis before any physical adjustments are made.

Zhang et al. focused on DT‑enabled optimal reconfiguration of a semi‑automatic electronic assembly line with frequent changeovers, explicitly optimizing reconfiguration decisions to handle high changeover frequency [21]. Their results demonstrate improvements in throughput and reductions in downtime when DT‑based optimization is used to select reconfiguration strategies, particularly under frequent product switches. This directly reinforces the manuscript’s emphasis on minimizing setups and reconfiguration time/cost in MPFP, as frequent part‑family changes can otherwise lead to excessive downtime and reduced capacity utilization [21]. Zhang et al. provided empirical evidence that DT‑enabled optimization of reconfiguration policies yields tangible operational benefits, supporting the manuscript’s intended impact on delivery performance and production continuity.

A dynamic layout optimization method of reconfigurable robotic assembly cells used DT models as the environment in which agents learn and evaluate layout changes [22]. Their results showed that multi‑agent learning can discover dynamic layouts that improve performance metrics. Although their focus was on layout optimization rather than explicit RP sequences, the underlying principle that DTs can host learning‑based optimization of reconfiguration decisions extends this conceptual framework. It suggests that the proposed DT architecture for RP evaluation could be augmented with multi‑agent or swarm‑based learning modules to automatically generate and refine RPs for MPFP in RFL [22].

Huang et al. proposed a DRL‑based dynamic reconfiguration planning approach for DT‑driven smart manufacturing systems with RMTs [23]. Their framework integrated process planning, reconfiguration, and scheduling, and uses DRL to learn policies that balance reconfiguration cost, time, and production performance. The reported results indicate that DRL‑based policies can outperform heuristic baselines in terms of throughput and responsiveness to changing demands [23]. The study demonstrated that DT‑driven reconfiguration planning can be coupled with advanced learning algorithms. This provided a clear future direction for extending the proposed RP framework from rule‑based or heuristic evaluation toward learning‑based policy optimization in MPFP contexts [23].

In this context, the proposed framework can be viewed as a synthesis and extension of prior DT‑driven RMS research works, adopts the proven benefits of DT‑based reconfiguration decision support [15], [16], [17], [21], incorporates predictive and evaluative metrics aligned with time and cost considerations [18], [21], and positions itself to integrate emerging optimization and learning approaches for dynamic, data‑driven RP selection in future work [19], [22], [23]. The manuscript addresses a practically important yet under‑specified decision problem in RMS, and its DT‑driven RP framework is well grounded in, and meaningfully connected to, the core results of the past studies [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23].

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p: This work presents a novel methodology for MPFP on an RFL by integrating a DT-driven RP with the RMS. Multiple, dissimilar part families each requiring distinct operations and operation sequences are processed across the four production stages of the RFL. When reconfiguration is necessary, existing RMT configurations on the stages are converted to new configurations between the completion and start of the next part family. For a predetermined part-family production order, the RP for each required transition is evaluated using the number of reconfiguration setups, reconfiguration time, and reconfiguration cost.

The DT-driven RP is proposed to continuously collect and process real‑time shop‑floor data into a Knowledge Database (data cleaning, mapping, data‑mining and machine learning). This data‑driven decision loop is developed to perform a predictive assessment of whether an RMT changeover is required, quantify trade‑offs among alternative RMT configurations (production rates, installation/removal costs), and select the configuration that minimizes changeovers, time, and cost while meeting operational requirements. For each pair of consecutive part families in the predetermined production order, the DT-based procedure compares the feasible reconfiguration policies and identifies the policy with the lowest reconfiguration burden; part families with distinct requirements trigger partial or full reconfigurations, with the DT-monitoring execution and updating the Knowledge Database to refine future decisions.

The proposed work is designed to improve responsiveness, reduce needless reconfigurations, and may support informed scheduling decisions under realistic, data‑driven constraints and can support managers in evaluating trade-offs among alternative RPs and selecting the most suitable choices for MPFP. Three RPs are evaluated in Table 7, Table 8, and Table 9. The selected RPs supports tactical production management by optimizing resource allocation, minimizing unnecessary setups, balancing reconfiguration time and cost with production needs, and improving capacity utilization, delivery reliability, downtime control, and operational continuity, although these benefits require empirical validation.

sec.title: 8. Limitation and future work
sec.p: The manuscript focuses on framework design, required data flows, and decision logic rather than a detailed implementation or experimental deployment. The present study has the following limitations:
• a single illustrative case evaluating only three RPs
• use of deterministic inputs
• absence of physical deployment
• lack of validation of DT fidelity
• limited problem scale
• omission of human and organizational factors
• dependence on validated shop‑floor data

The manuscript’s contributions lie in the illustrated conceptual architecture that formalizes RP selection, integrates DT‑based data flows, and structures managerial decision logic. Outcomes such as real‑time DT synchronization, autonomous policy updates, and learning‑enabled adaptation remain future implementation effects that require empirical testing. This now separates these two layers to clarify what is already established versus what must be demonstrated in practical deployment.

Future extensions of this work may include optimization of MPFP sequences for seasonal or time‑varying part families and coupling the DT with simulation and optimization platforms such as Enterprise Dynamics, Tecnomatix Plant Simulation, and MATLAB to evaluate alternative schedules, validate reconfiguration policies, and identify globally optimal MPFP plans. The framework may be extended to cases in which the part-family production order is also a decision variable. In future, an implementation study in controlled experiments can be carried out that compare the DT‑driven adaptive policy against three baseline rules for e.g., fixed production order, minimum‑cost, and minimum‑time using identical input data and constraints for every simulation run. Each policy can be evaluated on the same demand profiles, machine capabilities, and reconfiguration matrices, with performance measured by total reconfiguration time, total reconfiguration cost, and number of reconfiguration setups. This can be accompanied with sensitivity analyses including discrete two‑level tests and continuous parameter sweeps by varying reconfiguration cost and family demand to assess the robustness of policy selection and to identify conditions where the adaptive approach provides clear advantages.
